teaching_brief.overall_narrative_arc: The unit moves from celebration to crisis to consolidation. It opens with the political settlement of 1660 and asks what the Restoration actually restored. It then walks through the religious code that excluded Dissenters, the foreign and domestic shocks of Plague, Fire and the Dutch wars, and the way succession anxiety boiled into the Popish Plot and Exclusion Crisis. From there students study the rich social and cultural world the same regime nurtured — theatre, science, coffee houses, building — and then follow English power overseas through the Navigation Acts, Bombay, Jamaica and the slave trade. The historic environment lesson uses Ham House to make the period tangible. The unit closes by judging Charles II's reign in the round so students can write substantiated 16-mark essays.

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students assume 1660 was a return to absolute monarchy and that the Civil War was 'forgotten'. In fact Parliament emerged stronger, taxation became a negotiated relationship, and unresolved tensions over religion and succession would explode in the Exclusion Crisis and 1688.
common_misconceptions.source: AQA principal examiner reports on Paper 2 Section B Option D Restoration England; Tim Harris, Restoration: Charles II and his Kingdoms

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students confuse 1665 (Plague) and 1666 (Fire) and assume one caused or cured the other. The plague was waning before the Fire began on 2 September 1666; the Fire did not 'burn out' the plague.
common_misconceptions.source: Royal Museums Greenwich, The Great Plague and The Great Fire of London; Museum of London Great Plague resources

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students think the Royal Society was a government department funded by the Crown. It was a private subscription society of gentlemen-amateurs that received a royal charter (1662) and royal interest, but no Treasury money — fellows paid their own way.
common_misconceptions.source: Royal Society 'History of the Royal Society'; History Today, The Royal Society's First Charter

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students over-romanticise the Restoration as a carefree party after Puritan austerity. Court culture was politically charged: mistresses had French diplomatic links, theatre was censored, and religious and party tensions ran underneath the wit.
common_misconceptions.source: AQA mark schemes for Paper 2B/D on Charles II's character and court; Royal Museums Greenwich, The Restoration

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students assume modern political parties existed throughout the period. Whig and Tory labels only emerge during the Exclusion Crisis (1679-81) as nicknames; they were factions, not parties, and most MPs sat without a label.
common_misconceptions.source: Tim Harris, Restoration revisionist scholarship; UK Parliament living-heritage 1660-1688 timeline

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students think Clarendon wrote it. The four laws (Corporation Act, Act of Uniformity, Conventicle Act, Five Mile Act) were driven by the Cavalier Parliament, not Clarendon, who actually favoured wider toleration.
common_misconceptions.source: UK Parliament, Act of Uniformity 1662 and 1660-1688 key dates; AQA mark scheme commentary on the religious settlement

examiner_signals_unit_specific.signal: The 16-mark historic environment essay (Ham House in 2026) demands explicit, repeated linkage between the site and wider Restoration developments — not a guidebook description. Top-band answers use site features as evidence for an argument about court politics, design, women's status or patronage.
examiner_signals_unit_specific.source: AQA scheme of assessment 4.4.2; AQA principal examiner reports on Paper 2 Section B

examiner_signals_unit_specific.signal: Describe Two Features (4 marks) requires two clearly separated features each given a supporting detail — students who blur features into one paragraph cap at 2 marks.
examiner_signals_unit_specific.source: AQA mark scheme for 8145/2B/D, June 2023 onwards

examiner_signals_unit_specific.signal: Explain Effects (8 marks) wants consequences, not narrative. Top answers build chains: event -> effect on group -> wider effect on society/politics, with at least two distinct effects developed.
examiner_signals_unit_specific.source: AQA principal examiner reports on Paper 2 Section B Option D

examiner_signals_unit_specific.signal: Significance questions reward importance both at the time and over time. For Restoration topics this often means tracing a 1660s event forward to 1688 or beyond.
examiner_signals_unit_specific.source: AQA principal examiner reports; spec section 4.4.2 Significance descriptors

historiography_notes: Tim Harris's revisionist work (Restoration, 2005; Revolution, 2006) reframes Charles II as a politically skilful king navigating real party formation rather than a 'merry monarch'.
Lisa Jardine on Wren and the rebuilding of London situates St Paul's and the City churches as scientific as well as architectural achievements.
Claire Tomalin on Pepys foregrounds the Diary as social history not just naval administration.
Use historiography sparingly — only where it sharpens an exam-relevant argument.
second_order_concepts_emphasis: Cause and consequence (Plague, Fire, Popish Plot)
Change and continuity (what 1660 changed and what it preserved)
Significance (why an event mattered then and over time)
Similarity and difference (court culture vs popular culture; pre-Fire vs post-Fire London)

lessons.title: The Road Back to the Throne: Restoration of the Monarchy 1660
lessons.description: Why Charles II was invited home — the legacy of Civil War and Commonwealth and the Declaration of Breda settlement.
spec_bullets_covered: Crown and Parliament: the legacy of the English Civil War and Commonwealth; the restoration of the monarchy
key_content: Death of Cromwell 1658 and collapse of the Protectorate under Richard Cromwell
General Monck's march south and the Convention Parliament of 1660
Declaration of Breda: indemnity, religious toleration, arrears of army pay, parliamentary settlement
Charles II's entry into London 29 May 1660 — public mood and limits of triumph
Act of Indemnity and Oblivion 1660 — regicides excluded, the body of Cromwell exhumed and hanged
What was actually restored: monarchy, House of Lords, Anglican Church; abolished prerogative courts and feudal tenures stayed gone
lessons.exam_focus: Effects of the Restoration settlement on government and the army

lessons.title: The Cavalier Parliament and the Religious Settlement
lessons.description: How the Cavalier Parliament locked Anglicanism back into law and which groups it pushed to the margins.
spec_bullets_covered: relations and issues with Parliament, finance and religion
key_content: Election of the Cavalier Parliament 1661 — overwhelmingly royalist and Anglican
The four laws known as the Clarendon Code: Corporation Act 1661, Act of Uniformity 1662, Conventicle Act 1664, Five Mile Act 1665
Great Ejection 1662: around 2,000 ministers expelled from the Church of England
Definition and treatment of Dissenters/Nonconformists — Quakers, Baptists, Presbyterians, Independents
Charles II's preference for toleration vs Parliament's hard line — the 1672 Declaration of Indulgence withdrawn 1673
Royal finance: customs, hearth tax, the chronic gap between income and need
lessons.exam_focus: Two features of the Clarendon Code

lessons.title: The Cabal, Party Politics and Rule Without Parliament
lessons.description: How Charles II governed in the 1670s — through a five-man inner circle, then alone after 1681.
spec_bullets_covered: the Cabal and 'Party politics'; rule without parliament from 1681
key_content: Fall of Clarendon 1667 after the Second Dutch War
The Cabal ministry: Clifford, Arlington, Buckingham, Ashley (later Shaftesbury), Lauderdale — what each contributed
Secret Treaty of Dover 1670: French subsidy, conversion clause, war on the Dutch
Test Act 1673 forces Catholics out of office — Clifford and James, Duke of York resign
Emergence of Court (Tory) and Country (Whig) factions during the Exclusion Crisis
Oxford Parliament 1681 dissolved after one week — Charles rules without Parliament 1681-85, financed by a new French subsidy
lessons.exam_focus: Effects of the Cabal on Charles II's government

lessons.title: Charles II: The King and His Court
lessons.description: Charles II's character, his court, royal mistresses and what 'court life' actually meant in the 1660s and 1670s.
spec_bullets_covered: Charles II's court: Charles II's character; court life, fashions and the role of the court
key_content: Charles II's character: charming, clever, cynical; lessons of exile in France and the Low Countries
The court at Whitehall — over 2,000 rooms, 1,000 staff, public and private spheres
Royal mistresses as political actors: Barbara Villiers (Castlemaine), Nell Gwyn, Louise de Kéroualle
Catherine of Braganza, Portuguese Catholic queen, childless — the seed of the succession crisis
French fashions: long wigs, vests (1666), heeled shoes, formal dance, Italian opera
Court culture as politics: who got near the king got patronage and place
lessons.exam_focus: Significance of court life for politics and culture

lessons.title: The Great Plague of 1665
lessons.description: Causes, contemporary explanations, official measures and consequences of London's last great plague.
spec_bullets_covered: Crisis: Great Plague of 1665; causes and contemporary views; measures to combat; records; results
key_content: Outbreak in St Giles spring 1665, peak August-September with 7,000+ weekly deaths
Bills of Mortality and parish records — what they show and what they hide
Contemporary causes: miasma, sin, the comet of 1664, conjunctions of planets — almost no germ theory
Measures: shutting up infected houses with red cross and 'Lord have mercy upon us', plague pits, killing dogs and cats, fires in streets, court flees to Oxford
Total deaths around 100,000 — perhaps a fifth of London's population
Pepys's Diary: a privileged eyewitness who stayed for work and commuted from Greenwich
lessons.exam_focus: The events of the Great Plague of 1665

lessons.title: The Great Fire of London 1666: Disaster and Reconstruction
lessons.description: How a bakery fire became a city-destroying inferno and what rose from the ashes under Wren.
spec_bullets_covered: Fire of London of 1666; causes and contemporary views; results and reconstruction
key_content: 2-6 September 1666: Pudding Lane bakery, Lord Mayor Bloodworth's fatal indecision, easterly winds, timber and pitch
Charles II and James, Duke of York take personal command of firefighting — gunpowder and demolition
Scale of destruction: 13,200 houses, 87 churches, St Paul's, the Royal Exchange, the Guildhall — four-fifths of the City
Contemporary views: arson by Catholics or Dutch — Robert Hubert hanged after a false confession; the Monument inscription
Rebuilding Acts 1667 and 1670: brick and stone, wider streets, regulated trades, but Wren's grand street plan rejected
Wren's 51 City churches and St Paul's Cathedral 1675-1710 — money from a coal tax
lessons.exam_focus: Whether the Fire's effects were more positive than negative for London

lessons.title: The Catholic Question: Popish Plot and Rye House Plot
lessons.description: How Titus Oates's lies and a real assassination plan brought England to the edge of revolution.
spec_bullets_covered: The Catholic question: plots, including Titus Oates and the Popish Plot and the Rye House Plot
key_content: Background: anti-Catholicism, fear of France, James's open Catholicism after 1673
Titus Oates and Israel Tonge fabricate the Popish Plot autumn 1678 — claim Jesuits will assassinate Charles
Murder of Sir Edmund Berry Godfrey October 1678 — magistrate who took Oates's deposition
Around 35 Catholics executed; mass hysteria sweeps the country
Rye House Plot 1683: real Whig conspiracy to ambush and kill Charles and James — Russell and Sidney executed
Aftermath: a Tory reaction, purge of corporations, Charles's authority restored

lessons.title: The Exclusion Crisis and the Succession
lessons.description: Three Parliaments, three Exclusion Bills and the birth of Whigs and Tories — could a Catholic king be stopped?
spec_bullets_covered: the Exclusion Bill, 1679; James, Duke of York; the succession issue
key_content: James, Duke of York: open Catholic from 1673, heir presumptive to a childless king
Three Exclusion Bills 1679, 1680, 1681 — would have barred James from the throne
Shaftesbury and the Whigs argue parliamentary right to determine succession
Tories defend hereditary right and the Anglican settlement
Charles dissolves the Oxford Parliament March 1681 — turning point
Monmouth (Charles's illegitimate Protestant son) as alternative heir — sidelined; later rebels in 1685
lessons.exam_focus: Whether the Exclusion Crisis was mainly about religion or about power

lessons.title: Restoration Stage, Coffee Houses and Women in Public Life
lessons.description: Theatres reopen, women perform on stage for the first time, and coffee houses become the engine of public news.
spec_bullets_covered: Restoration culture: Restoration comedy, theatres and playwrights; the role and status of women; coffee houses
key_content: 1660 patents to Killigrew (King's Company) and Davenant (Duke's Company) — only two licensed theatres in London
Women on stage from 1660-61: actresses including Nell Gwyn, Elizabeth Barry — replacing boys in female roles
Restoration comedy: Etherege, Wycherley, Congreve, Behn — wit, sex, social satire; the shock of female playwrights
Aphra Behn — first English woman to make a living from writing
Coffee houses from 1652 (London's first) — penny universities, news, business, political gossip; Charles II's failed ban 1675
Wider role and status of women: still under coverture in law but visible at court, on stage, in print
lessons.exam_focus: Significance of women appearing on the public stage from 1660

lessons.title: The Royal Society, Pepys and the New Science
lessons.description: How a group of London gentlemen built the world's leading scientific society under Charles II's patronage.
spec_bullets_covered: Charles II's patronage of the arts and sciences, including the Royal Society; Samuel Pepys; architecture and design, including Christopher Wren
key_content: First meeting Gresham College November 1660 after a lecture by Christopher Wren
Royal Charter 1662, second charter 1663 — 'Royal Society of London for Improving Natural Knowledge'
A private subscription society — fellows paid their own dues; no Treasury funding
Key figures: Wilkins, Boyle, Hooke, Wren, later Newton (President from 1703)
Pepys: fellow from 1665, President 1684-86, signs the imprimatur of Newton's Principia 1687
Wren beyond St Paul's: the Royal Observatory at Greenwich (founded 1675), Royal Hospital Chelsea, Trinity College Library Cambridge
lessons.exam_focus: Significance of royal patronage for the new science

lessons.title: Sea Power, the Navigation Acts and the Dutch Wars
lessons.description: How England fought three wars with the Dutch to control trade — and what mercantilism meant in practice.
spec_bullets_covered: Trade: mercantilism; the Navigation Acts and their impact
War: English sea power; naval warfare, including tactics and technology; conflict with the Dutch, including the Second and Third Dutch Wars; relations with Spain and France
key_content: Mercantilism: zero-sum view of trade; bullion, colonies, monopoly companies
Navigation Acts 1660, 1662, 1663 — only English/colonial ships in colonial trade; goods landed in England first
Second Dutch War 1665-67: early English success at Lowestoft; humiliation at the Medway 1667 when De Ruyter burned the fleet at Chatham
Treaty of Breda 1667 — England keeps New York, Dutch keep Suriname
Third Dutch War 1672-74: alongside France under the Treaty of Dover; ended early when Parliament forced peace
Naval technology: line-of-battle tactics, the three-deck ship of the line, Pepys's reforms of victualling and shipbuilding
lessons.exam_focus: Effects of the Navigation Acts on English trade and shipping

lessons.title: Empire, Slavery and the End of the Reign 1685
lessons.description: Bombay, Tangier, Hudson Bay and Jamaica — how England's overseas reach grew, on whose backs, and where the reign left the country.
spec_bullets_covered: Land: the powers of the East India Company; Bombay; Hudson Bay; Tangier; Captain Henry Morgan and Jamaica
key_content: Catherine of Braganza's dowry 1662: Bombay (Mumbai) and Tangier
East India Company: chartered 1600, given Bombay 1668, granted near-sovereign powers — fortifications, mint, justice
Hudson's Bay Company chartered 1670 — fur trade, English claim to North America
Jamaica seized 1655 (Cromwell), kept at Restoration; sugar, slavery, and Henry Morgan's privateering — Panama 1671
Royal African Company chartered 1660, refounded 1672 with James as governor — branded 'DY' on enslaved people; the slave trade as state policy
Final years 1681-85: Tory reaction, French subsidy, prosperity for some; Charles II dies February 1685 — succession passes to Catholic James II and the Glorious Revolution looms
lessons.exam_focus: Significance of the slave trade for English wealth and empire under Charles II

part_1_crown_parliament_plots_court.notes: Restoration of monarchy (L1); Parliament/finance/religion (L2); Cabal and party politics, rule without parliament (L3); succession issue (L8); Catholic plots (L7); Exclusion Bill and James (L8); court life and character (L4).

part_2_life_in_restoration_england.notes: Plague (L5); Fire and reconstruction (L6); comedy/theatres/women/coffee houses (L9); Royal Society/Pepys/Wren architecture (L10).

part_3_land_trade_war.notes: Land: East India Company, Bombay, Hudson Bay, Tangier, Morgan, Jamaica all in L13. Trade: mercantilism and Navigation Acts in L11; slave trade in L13. War: sea power, Dutch wars, Spain/France in L11.

part_4_historic_environment.notes: Ham House (2026 site) treated against all required aspects: location, function, structure, people, design, cultural reflection, connection to wider events, change/continuity.

gaps.issue: L5 lists measures but examiner reports often want students to evaluate whether the measures helped at all. Worth flagging in content agent prompt so the lesson does not read like a list of rules.

Lauderdale's role at Ham House is easier to teach if students know he was widely hated in Scotland for the Highland Host and persecution of Covenanters. The spec does not require Scotland but L3 (Cabal) and L12 (Ham House) should reference it briefly.

Pepys's reform of the Navy Office (victualling, professional officer corps) is critical to L11 sea power but only listed as 'Pepys' in the spec (Part 2). Cross-link L10 and L11 so it does not get lost.

gaps.topic: Why coffee houses worried the Crown
gaps.issue: L9 should make explicit Charles II's 1675 attempted ban — students often miss that coffee houses were treated as politically dangerous, not just trendy.

L13 must handle the slave trade with appropriate seriousness for Year 11 students; it is the single most ethically demanding topic in the unit. Content agent should be told to present the human cost, not only the commercial gain.

site_2026.location: Richmond-upon-Thames, Surrey, on the south bank of the River Thames
site_2026.confirmed_source: AQA News — GCSE History: Historic environment sites 2026-2028 (aqa.org.uk/news/gcse-history-historic-environment-sites-2026-2028)
site_2026.site_summary: A Jacobean mansion remodelled and lavishly extended in the early 1670s by Elizabeth Murray (Countess of Dysart) and her second husband John Maitland, Duke of Lauderdale, a key member of Charles II's Cabal and Secretary of State for Scotland. Charles II created them Duke and Duchess of Lauderdale and granted Elizabeth a £800 annual pension after the Restoration. The Lauderdales doubled the building southward, installed a suite of rooms intended for Queen Catherine of Braganza, and filled the house with the latest French-influenced fashions, paintings, mirrored cabinets, parterre gardens and household inventories that survive almost untouched.
key_features_to_teach: Location on the Thames between Richmond and Hampton Court — close to the royal court but a private retreat
Function as a Restoration political household: Lauderdale entertained the king's inner circle here while running Scotland
Structure: Jacobean H-plan core (1610) extended south in 1672-74 to create the new state apartments
People connected: Elizabeth Murray, Duchess of Lauderdale; the Duke of Lauderdale; Charles II and Catherine of Braganza as visitors
Design: Long Gallery, Queen's Closet, Cabinet of Miniatures, sleeping arrangements that mirror Versailles court etiquette
How design reflects culture: French baroque taste, Restoration colour and gilding, scagliola, ebony and silver — wealth and proximity to the king as status symbols
Garden: parterre, wilderness and Cherry Garden show the new formal landscape style imported with Charles II from continental exile
Connection to wider events: the Cabal, Lauderdale's hard-line Scottish policy, court intrigue, female agency at the highest political level
links_back_to_period: Court culture and royal favour as the engine of social mobility (Part 1: Charles II's court; Part 2: court fashions)
The Cabal and patronage politics of the early 1670s (Part 1: Crown and Parliament)
Restoration architecture, design and decorative arts (Part 2: architecture and design, Wren parallel)
Status and influence of women in Restoration society (Part 2: role and status of women)
Wealth flowing from trade, slavery and overseas land grants into elite consumption (Part 3: trade, mercantilism)
